We use queries from C OUNTER FACT (Meng et al., 2022a).

threats_not_stated_by_authors: Architecture mismatch: evidence comes from GPT-2/GPT-J, not Gemma 4 E2B; KV-shared layers 15-34 and per-layer embeddings may change where subject enrichment and extraction occur.
Attention knockout may not transfer cleanly to grouped-query/KV-shared attention, where blocking edges and head roles differ from GPT-style MHSA.
The study conditions on correct predictions only, so it may miss failure modes and recall mechanisms relevant to factual-recall tracing.
Vocabulary projection/logit lens is approximate, especially in early layers, and may misestimate per-layer embeddings in Gemma.
Knowledge-head mapping uses top-10 token approximation and does not establish causal use of those heads during inference.
CPU-only activation patching/logit lens on Gemma 4 E2B may be limited by compute, requiring smaller samples and fewer intervention layers.
data.relevance_to_lab: Provides methods and findings for factual recall via attention knockout, logit-lens-style projection, MLP enrichment, and attention-head subject-attribute mappings; directly informs activation patching/logit lens/factual-recall tracing, but must be adapted to Gemma 4 E2B KV-shared layers 15-34 and per-layer embeddings on CPU.

data.title: Dissecting Recall of Factual Associations in Auto-Regressive Language Models
data.research_question: How do auto-regressive language models aggregate subject and relation information during factual recall, where is subject knowledge enriched, and which components extract the requested attribute?

models_and_data.quote: Both models use a vocabulary with ∼50K tokens.
Also, GPT-J employs parallel MHSA and MLP sublayers
We use queries from C OUNTER FACT (Meng et al., 2022a).
For a given model, we extract a random sample of queries for which the model predicts the correct attribute.
This results in 1,209 queries for GPT-2 and 1,199 for GPT-J.

For a given subject s, we first create a set As of candidate attributes, by retrieving paragraphs about s from Wikipedia using BM25 (Robertson et al., 1995), tokenizing each paragraph, and removing common words and sub-words.

protocol.step: Apply Attention Knockout to test direct propagation from subject and relation positions to the final position.
protocol.quote: We use Attention Knockout to test whether and, if so, where information from the subject and relation positions directly propagates to the last position.

protocol.step: Block attention edges over model-specific layer windows.
Apply Sublayer Knockout to test which sublayers enrich the last-subject representation.
protocol.quote: Concretely, we zero-out updates to the last subject position from each MHSA and MLP sublayer, for 10 consecutive layers.

protocol.step: Project hidden representations to vocabulary tokens as a logit-lens readout.
protocol.quote: To do this, we map hidden representations to vocabulary tokens via projection.

protocol.step: Compute attributes rate from the top projected tokens at the last-subject position across layers.
protocol.quote: We measure the attributes rate in the top k = 50 tokens by the subject representation, that is, the representation at the last-subject position, in each layer.

protocol.step: Measure layer-wise extraction for MHSA and MLP updates, including attention-blocked variants.
protocol.quote: Fig. 5 shows the extraction rate (namely the fraction of queries for which there was an extraction event) for the MHSA and MLP updates across layers in GPT-2, and Tab. 2 provides per-example extraction statistics

protocol.step: Patch early-layer subject representations into later MHSA layers and measure extraction-rate changes.
protocol.quote: For each layer ℓ = 0, 1, 5, 10, 20, with 0 being the embeddings, we feed the representations at the subject positions as input to the MHSA at any succeeding layer ℓ′ > ℓ.

protocol.step: Search attention-head parameter mappings for subject-attribute correspondences.
protocol.quote: For every extraction event with a subject s and an attribute a, we then check if a appears in the top-10 tokens for any of s’s tokens.

metrics.name: Relative change in prediction probability
metrics.definition: Percentage change in the probability of the correct predicted attribute after attention-edge interventions.
metrics.quote: Relative change in the prediction probability when intervening on attention edges to the last position, for window sizes of 9 layers in GPT-2 and 5 in GPT-J.

metrics.name: Attributes rate
metrics.definition: Fraction of a candidate attribute-token set that occurs among the top tokens predicted from a subject representation.
metrics.quote: the rate of the predicted attributes in a given set of tokens known to be highly related to the subject.

metrics.name: Attribute extraction rate
metrics.definition: Fraction of queries with at least one extraction event.
metrics.quote: Extraction rate here refers to the fraction of queries for which there was an extraction event in at least one layer.

metrics.name: Extraction event
metrics.definition: Agreement between the top token produced by a layer's sublayer update and the model's final top prediction.
metrics.quote: We check the agreement between t∗ and t′ for every ℓ ∈ [1, L], and refer to agreement cases (i.e., when t′ = t∗ ) as extraction events, since the attribute is being extracted by the MHSA.

metrics.name: Attribute rank
metrics.definition: Rank of the requested attribute under the vocabulary projection of the subject representation at an extraction event.
metrics.quote: We observe an average attribute rank of 999.5, which shows that the extraction operation promotes the specific attribute over many other candidate tokens.

metrics.name: Gradient-times-Input saliency
metrics.definition: Per-token saliency score computed from gradient-times-input, using L2-normalized vectors and normalization across tokens.
metrics.quote: a method such as Gradient-times-Input (Denil et al., 2014) reflects saliency: it shows (approximately) how much each input contributes to this particular logit value.

key_results.claim: Relation-position information reaches the prediction before subject-position information; blocking relation edges reduces prediction probability by 35%-45%.
key_results.quote: Moreover, another substantial decrease of 35%-45% is observed for the non-subject positions (dashed purple lines). Importantly, critical information from non-subject positions precedes the propagation of critical information from the subject positions

key_results.claim: Blocking subject-to-prediction attention in middle-upper layers sharply reduces factual prediction probability.
key_results.quote: For both GPT-2 and GPT-J, blocking attention to the subject tokens (solid green lines) in the middle-upper layers causes a dramatic decrease in the prediction probability of up to 60%.

key_results.claim: The last-subject representation becomes progressively enriched with subject-related attributes and substantially exceeds other positions.
key_results.quote: the attributes rate at the last-subject position is increasing throughout the layers, and is substantially higher than at other positions in the intermediate-upper layers, reaching close to 50%.

key_results.claim: Early MLP sublayers are the primary source of subject-representation enrichment, while MHSA cancellation has a smaller effect.
key_results.quote: canceling the early MLP sublayers has a destructive effect on the subject representation’s attributes rate, decreasing it by ∼88% on average. In contrast, canceling the MHSA sublayers has a much smaller effect of <30% decrease

key_results.claim: Upper MHSA sublayers perform attribute extraction for a majority of examples.
key_results.quote: When attending to all the input positions, the upper MHSA sublayers promote the attribute to the prediction (Fig. 5), with 68.2% of the examples exhibiting agreement events (Tab. 2).

key_results.claim: MLP sublayers also perform extraction, but substantially less often than MHSA sublayers.
key_results.quote: The extraction rate by the MLP sublayers is substantially lower (31.3%) than by the MHSA.

key_results.claim: Patching early subject representations reduces later extraction, demonstrating that subject enrichment is causally important for factual recall.
key_results.quote: Patching early subject representations decreases the extraction rate by up to 50%, which stresses the importance of attributes enrichment for attribute recall.

key_results.claim: Some extraction events are mediated by individual attention heads whose parameters encode the relevant subject-attribute mapping.
key_results.quote: We find that for 30.2% (39.3%) of the extraction events in GPT-2 (GPT-J), there is a head that encodes the subject-attribute mapping in its parameters (see examples in §G).

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: Vocabulary-space projection is used to interpret intermediate representations and parameters.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: Some of our experiments rely on interpreting intermediate layer representations and parameters through projection to the vocabulary space.

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: The projection-based interpretation is only an approximation, particularly in early layers.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: it only provides an approximation of the information encoded in these vectors, especially in early layers.

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: Attention knockout does not account for information leakage across positions.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: our attention knockout intervention method does not account for “information leakage” across positions.

limitations_stated_by_authors.text: The authors mitigate leakage by blocking ranges of layers rather than a single layer.
limitations_stated_by_authors.quote: For this reason, we block a range of layers rather than a single layer, which alleviates the possibility for such leakage.

threats_not_stated_by_authors: Only GPT-2 and GPT-J are tested, so the reported layer-by-layer mechanism may not transfer to Gemma 4 E2B, especially when KV sharing couples layers 15-34 and changes the effective independence of heads and sublayers.
COUNTERFACT is a templated factual dataset, and restricting analysis to queries already answered correctly creates success-selection bias and excludes failed, ambiguous, or competing-answer recalls.
The BM25 Wikipedia candidate sets use token overlap as a proxy for semantic relatedness and may reward corpus-frequency associations rather than subject-specific factual knowledge.
The authors do not test whether vocabulary projection remains a valid readout for Gemma's embedding geometry, vocabulary composition, or multilingual tokenization.
The experiments cover short single-relation prompts, without testing multi-hop facts, distractors, paraphrases, long contexts, multilingual facts, or robustness to prompt format.
Exact top-1 agreement can miss near-correct answers, subword-prefix attributes, or distributed extraction, so extraction rate may not measure graded factual recall.
The Wikipedia dump used to construct candidate attributes is dated and may not match the pretraining corpus or factual state represented by a newer model.
No runtime or memory analysis is provided, and dense head searches plus repeated per-layer interventions on a 6B model do not directly indicate what is feasible for CPU-only experiments.
data.relevance_to_lab: The paper is highly relevant methodologically: attention-edge knockouts, sublayer cancellation, vocabulary projection of per-layer embeddings, early-to-late activation patching, and attention-head parameter mapping can be transferred to Gemma 4 E2B factual-recall tracing. Its central hypothesis for the lab is that lower layers enrich a subject representation while later layers query that representation to extract the requested attribute, motivating separate patching of relation, last-subject, other subject, and final-position activations in layers 15-34. Gemma's shared-KV architecture requires adapting the intervention and layer accounting rather than directly adopting GPT layer indices. Head-level subject-attribute analysis can also complement induction-head tracing, while keeping the two head functions conceptually distinct. Given CPU-only execution, a practical starting point is a small factual set, cached per-layer embeddings, sparse layer windows, and selected candidate heads, followed by checks for whether shared-KV behavior changes the predicted relation-to-subject flow.
